clue.text: I mainly encountered round fish in drink

indicators.note: mainly here stands for the chief or leading part, so only the head of each of the opening words counts
round means surrounding, so the selected letters go on either side of the next piece

blocks.note: the leading letters of the three words I, mainly and encountered
the bib, or pouting, is a small fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Someone recounts meeting a round fish while having a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbibe is to take in liquid, especially alcohol, so it works as the verb sense of drink.

clue.text: Most of ivy is nice; if rambling, the answer's cutting

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept
something rambling wanders about with no fixed course, so the letters wander out of order

blocks.note: the plant's name without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener muses that ivy looks pleasant when it rambles over a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutting remark is sharp and penetrating, which is exactly what an incisive one is.

clue.text: Disease of fruit, we're told repeatedly

indicators.note: we're told means we hear it spoken, so the spelling follows the sound rather than the word

blocks.note: a small soft fruit, written to match how it is pronounced
the same sound said a second time

explanation.surface: A plant disease is reported again and again in a crop of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: The name of the disease comes from Sinhalese and sounds like the fruit said twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Beriberi is a nutritional illness caused by a lack of vitamin B1, thiamine.

clue.text: Kentish area in chance attack

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the area sits within the word for a chance

blocks.note: a bet is a wager, taking a chance
Kent is a county in the south-east of England, abbreviated SE

explanation.surface: A raid launched on a corner of Kent by sheer luck.
explanation.definitionFit: To beset is to assail or harass from all sides, so it is a verb meaning to set upon.

clue.text: One in a row put in dries out

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of order or wrong, so its letters are rearranged
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Instructions for laundry: put clothes in and the dryer finishes them off.
explanation.walkthrough: Row here rhymes with cow: a quarrel, not a line of things.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone engaged in an argument or quarrel is one who disputes, a person arguing a point.

clue.text: Brainwashed? Not I - and with credit in order

indicators.note: putting letters in order implies they arrive jumbled and must be sorted into a new sequence

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protests they were not brainwashed, and gives credit for their views being orderly.
explanation.definitionFit: To indoctrinate is to instil fixed beliefs uncritically, the same as having one's mind conditioned.

clue.text: Dreamy chap, not a bastard; he's thick-skinned

indicators.note: not tells us to leave out the following little word
bastard as an adjective means debased or impure, so the letters are corrupted into another form

blocks.note: taken as written
the article, to be removed

explanation.surface: A defence of a dreamy fellow: he is no rotter, just insensitive.
explanation.definitionFit: Pachyderms such as elephants are named for their thick hide; figuratively, an insensitive person.

clue.text: Make them run away

blocks.note: surface reading: frighten some people into fleeing
setter's reading: the idiom with make in front means to leave hastily, and these are also what trains run along

explanation.walkthrough: Them looks like people being chased off; it is the plural noun in the idiom make tracks, to depart quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom make tracks means to leave or hurry off, so the word completing it fits running away.

clue.text: Gold coins found in the Palace?

blocks.note: first meaning: old English gold coins, also spelt ryals, struck under Edward IV and later
second meaning: members of the monarch's family, who live at Buckingham Palace

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second half describes people rather than defining them.
explanation.definitionFit: A royal was a historic gold coin, and the plural is also informal for members of the royal family.

clue.text: The state of one's affairs when short

definitions.text: The state of one's affairs when short

blocks.clueFragment: The state of one's affairs when short
blocks.note: surface reading: how things stand for someone who is short of money
setter's reading: the word for one's situation, in its clipped informal form

explanation.walkthrough: Short suggests lacking cash; it means abbreviated, the clipped form of circumstances.
explanation.definitionFit: Circs is a colloquial British abbreviation of circumstances, meaning one's situation or condition.

clue.text: Unusual air about one seized by lady judges

indicators.note: unusual means out of the ordinary, so the letters appear in an unfamiliar arrangement
something seized is held in a grip, so these letters are clasped within the lady

blocks.note: Judy is a girl's name, and old slang for a woman
taken as written
c is short for circa, about
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A strange atmosphere surrounds a woman's courtroom ruling.
explanation.definitionFit: The judiciary is the collective body of judges in a legal system, the branch that judges cases.

clue.text: Skipping over the piece, acting prematurely

blocks.note: first meaning, taken literally: leaping over a firearm, since a piece is a gun
second meaning: the idiom for starting before the signal

explanation.walkthrough: Piece sounds like a chess or music piece; it is slang for a gun, which makes the literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from athletes starting before the starting pistol fires, so it means doing something too soon.

clue.text: Payment to a man in charge is very small

blocks.note: a sub is a subscription or an advance on wages
taken as written
Tom is a man's name, and also a male cat
i/c is the standard abbreviation for in charge

explanation.surface: A modest fee paid to the man in charge.
explanation.definitionFit: Subatomic describes particles smaller than an atom, so it suits anything extremely tiny.

clue.text: Country type: the old line's taken in all right

indicators.note: taken in means admitted inside, so the old line encloses the next piece

blocks.note: ye is the archaic spelling of the
L is the abbreviation for line
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A rustic remarks that the old railway line has been fine.
explanation.definitionFit: A yokel is a naive rural person, a disparaging term for a countryman.

clue.text: Tobacco waver taking part in country dance?

blocks.note: Virginia is a type of tobacco named after the US state
to reel is to stagger or sway unsteadily

explanation.surface: A smoker, unsteady on their feet, joins in a barn dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The Virginia reel is an American folk dance performed by couples in facing lines.

clue.text: Fuming about artist I'd backed to shine

indicators.note: backed means moved backwards, so the two letters of I'd run the other way
about means surrounding, so the angry word goes around the artist and the reversed word

blocks.note: fuming means very angry
RA is a Royal Academician
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: An angry patron complains about an artist they once supported.
explanation.definitionFit: To irradiate is to shine light upon or illuminate, so it can stand for the verb shine.

clue.text: Restrict the way by the river to fish

blocks.note: St is short for street, a way
R is the abbreviation for river
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: A notice limits access to the riverside path for anglers.
explanation.definitionFit: To strangle something, such as trade or growth, is figuratively to suppress or choke it.

clue.text: Sketch of animal's brought up by little sister

indicators.note: in a down clue, brought up means read from the bottom upwards, so the word is reversed

blocks.note: pony's, a small horse's, without the apostrophe
sis is the familiar short form of sister

explanation.surface: A young girl draws a picture of her pet.
explanation.definitionFit: A synopsis is a brief outline or summary, and a sketch can mean a rough outline of a plan or story.

clue.text: For example, monitor involved in test for school subject

indicators.note: involved means intricate or tangled, so the letters are twisted together
in means placed inside the word for a test

blocks.note: e.g. is the abbreviation for for example
taken as written
a try is an attempt or test

explanation.surface: A class monitor takes part in an exam for a school subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening For belongs to the abbreviation; the second for is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Trigonometry, the mathematics of triangles and angles, is taught as part of maths at school.

clue.text: Pressure point up

blocks.note: first meaning: strain or force, as a noun
second meaning: to emphasise, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests a pressure point; the two halves are separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means strain or tension as a noun and, as a verb, to emphasise or highlight something.

clue.text: One using foil to repair enclosure?

blocks.note: first meaning: a swordsman, since a foil is a light fencing sword
second meaning, whimsically: someone who mends fences

explanation.walkthrough: Foil suggests kitchen wrap; it is the blunted sword used in the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A fencer practises swordplay with foil, épée or sabre, and literally could be a person who builds fences.

clue.text: The inclination to care is about right

indicators.note: about means around, so the caring word surrounds the letter for right

blocks.note: to tend is to care for
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone observes that the urge to look after others is basically sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A trend is a general direction or tendency, which is what an inclination is.

clue.text: Lancashire dish, one to produce a tricky problem

blocks.note: Lancashire hotpot is a lamb and potato stew from north-west England
a means one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook finds a regional stew a difficult dish to make.
explanation.definitionFit: A hot potato is an idiom for a controversial issue that is awkward to handle.

clue.text: Flowery, but not new, talk

indicators.note: not means without, so the abbreviation that follows is dropped

blocks.note: ornate means elaborately decorated, flowery
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A critic says a speech was florid but nothing novel.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to make a formal speech, often pompously, so it is a verb meaning to talk.

clue.text: Swapped old coins and old coins

blocks.note: ex means former
change is loose coins
d stood for pence in pre-decimal British money, from the Latin denarii

explanation.surface: A collector traded some antique coins for others.
explanation.walkthrough: The repetition of old coins looks lazy; each phrase gives a different piece, and d was the abbreviation for the old penny.
explanation.definitionFit: To exchange is to give one thing and receive another, which is what swapping means.

clue.text: Age is reconsidered in sponsorship

indicators.note: something reconsidered is thought through again and arranged anew, so the letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sponsor rethinks an age limit for their funding.
explanation.definitionFit: Under the aegis of someone means with their backing or protection, so it serves as sponsorship.

clue.text: Policeman wearing material and short trousers, initially

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the little word loses its tail

blocks.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled fabric used for uniforms
taken as written, then clipped
the first letter of trousers

explanation.surface: A police officer kitted out in heavy cloth and shorts.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a police rank above constable, so a sergeant is a kind of police officer.

clue.text: Splits continually seen in the ship

indicators.note: seen in means appearing inside, so the word sits within the ship abbreviation

blocks.note: ever means always, continually
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Cracks keep appearing in a vessel's hull.
explanation.definitionFit: To sever is to cut apart or divide, so severs means splits as a verb.
